offence_severity: Minimum 10 years to maximum death (Section 307 IPC) and 3 years to 7 years (Section 394 IPC) and 3 years (Section 25/27 Arms Act)
physical_harm: Injuries caused to the complainant, including pellets striking his forehead, left shoulder, and left ear, resulting in blood oozing
financial_property_loss: Rs. 7,300/-, two Nokia mobiles, Rs. 19,000/-, Rs. 16,500/-, and a Spice mobile
motive: Enmity and scuffle between the complainant's nephew and the accused
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the offences alleged were non-compoundable, had serious social impact, and were not private disputes. It emphasized that the High Court erred in mechanically quashing the FIRs without considering the gravity of the offences and the social impact.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the witnesses' statements were relevant, but the High Court did not properly evaluate their credibility in the context of the serious nature of the offences and the social impact.
post_offence_conduct: The accused were absconding and approached the High Court three months after the incident, which the Supreme Court considered relevant in assessing the credibility of their compromise and the necessity of proceeding with the criminal proceedings.
trial_duration: Offence: 21.12.2012; Trial judgment: Not stated; High Court: 15.03.2013; Supreme Court: February 22, 2019
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Varun K. Chopra, Mrs. Swarupama Chaturvedi, B. N. Dubey, Mukesh Kumar, Gurtej Pal Singh, Ms. Indira Bhakar, Ms. Aparna Trivedi, Santanu Singh Advs. Counsel for the State: Lakhan Singh Chouhan, Hitesh Kumar Sharma, Narender Singh, Baby Devi Bonia, Binay Kumar Das, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Quashed by High Court; High Court: Quashed by High Court; Supreme Court: Allowed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the High Court erred in quashing the FIRs as the offences alleged were non-compoundable and had serious social implications, and the High Court did not consider the gravity of the offences or the social impact.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court correctly quashed the FIRs based on the compromise between the accused and the complainant, and that the High Court's decision was in line with the precedent set in Shiji @ Pappu and others v. Radhika and another.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the High Court must evaluate whether the ends of justice would justify the exercise of its inherent power under Section 482 CrPC, and that serious offences against society cannot be quashed merely on the basis of a compromise.
precedent_relied_upon: Gian Singh v. State of Punjab (2012) 10 SCC 303; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Deepak (2014) 10 SCC 285; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Manish (2015) 8 SCC 307; Parbatbhai Aahir v. State of Gujarat (2017) 9 SCC 641; State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kalyan Singh [2019] 1 SCALE 165; State of Maharashtra v. Vikram Anantrai Doshi (2014) 15 SCC 29; Narinder Singh v. State of Punjab (2014) 6 SCC 466
